title: Running Design Critiques
intro: Name the meeting type first. Then run a timed slot with silent written feedback before the discussion.

learn.title: Four kinds of meeting
learn.text:
**Critique:** improve the craft. Questions, not instructions.
**Design review:** check against goals. Feedback is implemented or answered.
**Quality review:** keep the system consistent. Led by a lead, directive.
**Shareout:** show progress. One-way.

Most critique fights start because people expected a different meeting.

try.q: Feedback must be implemented or answered with a reason. Which meeting is this?
try.explain: In a critique the designer chooses what to use. In a design review each point gets an answer.

learn.title: The 30-minute slot
learn.text:
**2 min** background · **3 min** walkthrough · **2 min** clarifying questions only · **7–10 min of silent written feedback** · **10–13 min** conversation · **3 min** wrap-up.

Silent writing collects everyone’s view before one person anchors the room.

try.q: What comes right before the conversation?
try.explain: Everyone has written down their view, so the loudest voice doesn’t set the frame.

learn.title: Who speaks, and what to ask
learn.text:
Hear from other disciplines first, then designers, then leads.

Good questions: what is the main benefit for the user? What other ways would deliver it? Which decision are you least sure about? What happens when it goes wrong?

A polished mockup can hide missing decisions. Match the fidelity to how settled the idea is.

try.q: In the discussion, who speaks first?
options: The most senior lead in the room
The designer who made the work
try.explain: Seniority speaking last stops juniors simply agreeing.

test.q: How many people should be in a critique?
test.explain: More than six and the quiet people stop contributing.

test.q: When should the presenter share the topic?
options: At the start of the meeting
test.explain: People need time to look at the context, and the presenter states the feedback they want.

test.q: What kind of feedback does a critique ask for?
options: A numeric score for each screen
A plain yes or no on the design
test.explain: The designer decides what to use. Questions open the work up instead of closing it.

test.q: What is the form factor trap?
options: A polished artifact hides undecided questions
Testing on only one device size
Designing a form before the data model exists
Putting too many fields on a single form
test.explain: Fidelity should match how settled the idea is. If nobody can name the user benefit, that is a finding.

test.q: Why rotate roles like captain and note-taker?
options: So the same voices don’t dominate
To keep every meeting a bit shorter
To give design leads more control
To avoid having to write an agenda
test.explain: Rotation spreads ownership and keeps the room from relying on one person.
